DE LEON Human Resource Management, Officer IV Office of the Municipal Mayor Imus, Cavite Dear Ms. De Leon: This has reference to your earlier letter asking our opinion on the entitlement of back wages of Mayor Oscar A. Jaro of Imus, Cavite. Based on your letter, your query is whether or not Mayor Jaro, who later on won in the two (2) election protests, may still recover the salaries appurtenant to said office during the time that the same was held by Engr. Homer T. Saquilayan, the person who had been proclaimed as winner and had initially assumed said office but was later ousted as a result of the election protests. In reply to your query, we answer in the negative. Well-settled is the rule that a person acquires public office either by appointment or by election. An appointment is the act or designation by the executive officer, board or body to where that power has been delegated, of tne individual who is to exercise the functions of a given office (Mechem, Section 102). On the other hand, an election "Ineans thc choice or selection of candidates to public office by popular vote through the use of the ballot, anzi the elected officials are dcterlnined I•hrongh the will of the electorate. An election is the enzbodiment of the popular will, the expression of the sovereign poccer of the people. The winner is the candidate (Who has obtained a jnajority or plurality of valid votes cast in the election" (Rulloda vs. COMELEC, G.R. No. 154198, January 20, 2003).

There are instances however where one's acquisition of right or title to such public office would be challenged or questioned thereby giving rise to multiple and repetitious suits. In order to protect the public by insuring the orderly functioning of the government despite allegations of detect in title to office of the public officers, there is the so-called de lure doctnne/de facto doctrine in public office. In de lure doctrine, a person has the lawful right to the office in ail respects, but wno has either been ousted from it, or who has never actually taken possession of it. On the other hand, the de facto doctrine refers to the principle which holds that a person who, by the proper authority, is admitted and sworn into office is deemed to be rightfully in such office until, by judicial declaration in a proper proceeding, he is ousted therefrom, or his admission thereto is declared void (63A Am. Jur. 2d 1081 as cited in the Law on Public Officers and Election Law, de Leon and de Leon, Jr., 3' d ed., p. 106). A de facto officer is thus defined by the Supreme Court in the case of Torres vs. Ribo 81 Phil 44, as one who has the reputation of being the officer that he assumes to be, and yet is not a good officer in point of law. He must have acted as officer for such length of time, under color of titie and under such circumstances of reputation or acquiescence by the public and public authorities, as to afford a presumption of election or appointment, and induce people, without inquiry, and relying on the supposition that he is the officer he assumes to be, to submit to or invoke his action. Based on the foregoing, we can aptly say that Mayor Jaro is a dejure officer since he, after the two election protests were decided in his favor, has the lawful right to the office in all respects, but who has either been ousted from it, or who has never actually taken possession of it in conformity with the abovementioned definition of a de jure officer. On the other hand, Engr. Saquilayan can be properly considered as a de facto officer since he, by the proper authority, is sworn to and allowed to assume the mayoralty post, and is deemed to be rightfully in such office until, by judicial declaration in a proper proceeding, he is ousted therefrom, or his admission thereo is declared void in conformity with the abovementioned definition of a de facto officer. Coming now to your query, may we invite your attention to the pronouncements made by the Supreme Court in the cases of Rodriquez vs. Tan, 91 Phil 724 and Malaluan vs. COMELEC G.R. No. 120193 March 6 1996.

In the case of Rodriquez vs. Tan, supra., Carlos Tan was proclaimed as one of those elected as Senators by the COMELEC in the II November 1947 elections and immediately entered into the performance of the duties of the position, after taking his oath of office thereto. Eulogio Rodriguez filed an election protest before the Senate Electoral Tribunal and said body rendered a judgment declaring Rodriguez to have been duly elected to office. Thus, Rodriguez sought for the collection of salaries and allowances appurtenant to the office of the Senator during the time that Tan held the same. The Supreme Court decided in the following manner and we quote: "xxx There is no question that the defendant (Tan) acted as a de facto officer during the tinze Ize held the office of Senator. Having been thus duly proclai;ugd as Senator and having assunzed office as required bU loco, it cannot be disputed that defendant is entitled to the conzpensation, enzolu;nents and allowances which our Constitution provides Tor the position (Article VI, Section 14). This is as it should be. This is in keeping 11'itJz the ordinary course of events. This is silliple justice. This is the policy and the rule that has been follozped consistentlu_ in this iurisdiction in connection (Fith positions held by goho had beeg eleg$ed thereto but roere later o.ysfcd gsg result of election protest. The right Of thc' persons elected to contpenstLtion during their incunlbencl/ alzoavs been recognized=_ We cannot recall ani/ precedent (Ql.wrein tlze con rule has been upheld." (Emphasis Supplied) The foregoing ruling of the Supreme Court was reiterated in the later case of Malaluan vs. COMELEC, supra. The Supreme Court held therein and we quote: "The long-standing rule in this jurisdiction is that notwithstanding his subsequent ouster as a result of an election protest, an elective official who has been proclaimed by the COMELEC as coinner in an electoral contest and coho assunred office ancl entered into the perfonnance of the duties of that office, is entitled to the contpensation, euroluntents and allotoanccs legally provided for the position.

In view of the foregoing, we are of the opinion that Mayor Jaro may no longer recover the salaries appurtenant to the Office of the Mayor during the time that said position was held by Engr. Saquilayan, the person who had been proclaimed as winner and had initially assumed said office but was later ousted as a result of the election protests. We hope that we have addressed your concern accordingly. Ver truly yours, AUST RE A. PANADE O OIC, OUSLG L/' Legal/17
